title: I Am Joseph — the Cry, the Recognition, the Sending
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. We can all recite the line about forgiving seventy times seven. And yet there is a telephone call that some of us have not made in twenty years.

We say it to ourselves: I don't hate him, I simply don't want anything more to do with him. Brothers and sisters, deleting a person from your heart is not forgiveness. That is severance. Forgiveness is putting that person back into the relationship.

In Genesis chapter 45, Joseph finally opens his mouth. He has waited twenty-two years; he has waited two whole chapters. And at this moment he holds absolute authority, with a roomful of Egyptian officials standing at his elbow.

And the first thing he does is drive every Egyptian out of the room. The first thing he says is, "I am Joseph!" And the first question he asks is not "How could you have done that to me?" — it is, "Does my father still live?"
1. Cause Everyone to Go Out from Me

"Then Joseph couldn't control himself before all those who stood before him, and he called out, 'Cause everyone to go out from me!' No one else stood with him, while Joseph made himself known to his brothers." (Genesis 45:1)

"Couldn't control himself" is לְהִתְאַפֵּק (*lehitapeq*) in the original — the very word from chapter 43, where he "controlled himself" by force. Literally it means to band yourself tight, to hold yourself in. Last time he held. This time he cannot.

"Made himself known" is בְּהִתְוַדַּע (*behitvada*), literally "to cause himself to be recognised." And what he did back in chapter 42 was וַיִּתְנַכֵּר (*vayitnaker*), "he made himself a stranger." The same grammatical form, pointing in exactly the opposite direction.
Now I want you to think for a moment about his clearing the room.

The men standing there are Egyptian officials, scribes, guards. If Joseph wanted revenge, this is the perfect moment — say the truth out loud in front of them all: these eleven men are the ones who sold me twenty-two years ago.
They would be ruined — name, standing, everything. And it would be entirely legal, and entirely just.
But he sends every one of them out. What he is about to say, he does not want outsiders to hear.
Brothers and sisters, the first mark of forgiveness is that it protects the other person's dignity.
This is a very practical matter. To find out whether you have truly forgiven someone, you do not need to ask what you feel. Ask your mouth: are you still telling other people what he did?
As long as that matter is still material for your conversation, the forgiveness is not finished.
"He wept aloud. The Egyptians heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard." (Genesis 45:2)

"He wept aloud" is וַיִּתֵּן אֶת־קֹלוֹ בִּבְכִי (*vayiten et-qolo bivchi*) in the original, literally "he gave his voice over to weeping." This is not quiet sobbing. This is a man weeping until his voice breaks.
He drives them all out, the door closes — and then he weeps until the people on the other side of that door can hear him. Twenty-two years of it, poured out all at once.
"Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am Joseph! Does my father still live?'" (Genesis 45:3)
In the original it is two words: אֲנִי יוֹסֵף (*ani Yosef*).
And what comes straight after is not an accusation. It is "Does my father still live?" — in the original הַעוֹד אָבִי חָי (*ha'od avi chai*), "Is my father still alive?"
He already knows the answer. In the previous chapter Judah spoke for seventeen verses, and every sentence of it was about the father. When Joseph asks this, he is not asking for information.
He is a son who has not seen his father for twenty-two years. He is making sure of something he does not dare to believe.
And the text says, "His brothers couldn't answer him; for they were terrified at his presence."
"Terrified" is נִבְהֲלוּ (*nivhalu*) in the original, and it is a violently strong word — the shock of a thunderclap, the soul knocked clean out of the body.
Verse 1 says Joseph "couldn't" control himself; verse 3 says they "couldn't" answer him. In that one room, both sides have lost control.
Why did he drive all the Egyptians out?

The men standing there were Egyptian officials, scribes and guards. If he had wanted revenge, that was the perfect moment — say the truth out loud in front of them all: these eleven men are the ones who sold me twenty-two years ago. They would have been ruined, and it would have been entirely legal and entirely just. But he sends every one of them out; what he is about to say, he does not want outsiders to hear. The first mark of forgiveness is that it protects the other person's dignity. And this is a very practical matter: to find out whether you have truly forgiven someone, do not ask what you feel — ask your mouth. Are you still telling other people what he did? As long as that matter is still material for your conversation, the forgiveness is not finished.
"I am Joseph! Does my father still live?" — he plainly knows the answer already. Why does he ask?

In the previous chapter Judah spoke for seventeen verses and every sentence of it was about the father, so of course he knows. When he asks this, he is not asking for information. He is a son who has not seen his father for twenty-two years, and he is making sure of something he does not dare to believe. And notice where this sentence falls. The first thing out of his mouth is not the accusation "How could you have done that to me?" — it is the question whether his father is still alive. The sentence that surfaces first in a person's heart is the most honest one he has. Twenty-two years of power, position and glory are in his hands, and the first thing he thinks of is the old man at home.
Does deleting a person from your heart count as forgiveness?

No. That is severance. Forgiveness is putting that person back into the relationship. We often say to ourselves, "I don't hate him, I simply don't want anything more to do with him." It sounds very mature; more often than not it is only the account being sealed up and filed away. This chapter gives forgiveness a very concrete shape: do not expose him in public, do state the fact plainly, and then say, "Come near to me, please." Of course that does not mean every relationship must be restored to its old closeness — in chapter 31 Jacob and Laban could only stop at Mizpah. The test is this: in my heart, am I still collecting on that debt? If I am, it is not finished. If I am not, then even distance can be kind.
2. A Light from the Original: Come Near to Me, Please
"Joseph said to his brothers, 'Come near to me, please.' They came near." (Genesis 45:4)
"Come near to me, please" is גְּשׁוּ־נָא אֵלַי (*geshu-na elai*) in the original. That little נָא (*na*) is the Hebrew softening particle, and it turns a command into an invitation.
He is the ruler of Egypt. He could give an order. What he says is "please."
Brothers and sisters, this is the gentlest sentence in the whole chapter. They are backing away in terror, and he says: come, come a little closer.
And what he says next is this: "I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt."
He does not blur it. "Whom you sold" — אֲשֶׁר־מְכַרְתֶּם (*asher-mechartem*) — the fact is stated with perfect clarity.
This matters enormously. Forgiveness is not pretending the thing never happened. He states the fact, and then he says: now, come closer.
And then comes the theological heart of this chapter:

"Now don't be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life … God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance. So now it wasn't you who sent me here, but God." (Genesis 45:5–8)
Three times over: God sent me.
"Sent" is שָׁלַח (*shalach*) in the original. The subject of that verb is God.
And "it wasn't you … but God" — לֹא־אַתֶּם … כִּי הָאֱלֹהִים (*lo-atem … ki ha'Elohim*) — is the governing sentence of the whole chapter.
Brothers and sisters, here I want to explain something very carefully, because this verse has been misused far too often.
Joseph is not saying, "You did nothing wrong." One verse earlier he has just said, "whom you sold into Egypt"; and in chapter 50 he will still say, "As for you, you meant evil against me."

Human evil is real evil, and God's sovereignty is still greater — both sentences have to be said at once. Leave out the first and you have cheap papering-over. Leave out the second and there is no way out.
And notice who has the standing to say it. The one speaking is the victim himself, and he is speaking twenty-two years afterwards.

This sentence was never meant to be picked up by bystanders and used to stop a suffering person's mouth. If somebody is in the middle of the pain and you walk over and say, "God meant it for good" — that is not comfort. That is dismissal.
This sentence can only come out of the mouth of the person it happened to, and usually only a very long time afterwards.

There is one more word well worth looking at. "A remnant" is שְׁאֵרִית (*she'erit*) in the original — what is left over, the ones who survive. This is the first seed of the Old Testament's whole theology of the remnant. Isaiah later, and Jeremiah, and Paul, all use this word for the small group God keeps for himself in the worst of years.
What God saves here is not only one man; it is a family. And not only a family; it is the Saviour who would one day come out of that family.

"Don't be grieved, nor angry with yourselves" — the root behind "grieved" is the very word for the "pain" laid on Adam and Eve under the curse in chapter 3; and "angry with yourselves" is literally "let it not burn in your eyes," that is, do not be furious with yourselves.
Brothers and sisters, there are people who, once they have been forgiven, find that the hardest person to let off is themselves. Joseph thought even of that for them.
"Come near to me, please" — why is that the gentlest sentence in the chapter?

The "please" in the original is the Hebrew softening particle, and it turns a command into an invitation. He is the ruler of Egypt; he could give an order. What he says is "please." And remember what state they are in at that moment — "terrified", and the Hebrew is a violently strong word, the shock of a thunderclap. They are backing away, and he says: come, come a little closer. That hands us something very practical. When you want to be reconciled to someone who is afraid of you, or who is ashamed before you, the tone matters more than the content. A command makes a person retreat further; only an invitation brings him near. And notice what he says next: the fact — "whom you sold into Egypt." He does not blur the truth to keep the atmosphere pleasant.
"It wasn't you who sent me here, but God" — may that sentence be said just anywhere?

No, it may not; this verse has been misused far too often. First, Joseph is not saying, "You did nothing wrong": one verse earlier he has just said "whom you sold into Egypt", and in chapter 50 he will still say, "As for you, you meant evil against me." Human evil is real evil, and God's sovereignty is still greater — both sentences have to be said at once; leave out the first and you have cheap papering-over, leave out the second and there is no way out. Second, notice who has the standing to say it: the one speaking is the victim himself, and he is speaking twenty-two years afterwards. This sentence was never meant to be picked up by bystanders and used to stop a suffering person's mouth.
3. Hurry, and Go Up to My Father
The tone of what Joseph says next changes completely. From verse 9 onwards it is all imperatives, and they come fast:
"Hurry, and go up to my father, and tell him, 'This is what your son Joseph says, "God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me. Don't wait."'" (Genesis 45:9)
"This is what your son Joseph says" is כֹּה אָמַר (*koh amar*) in the original — precisely the prophet's formula for carrying a message: "Thus says Yahweh."
That word "hurry" comes twice over in this chapter, in verse 9 and again in verse 13, and the whole speech runs at that pace. And "don't wait" is, in the original, "do not stand still."
He wants them living in the land of Goshen, where they will be "near to me." And he says, "There I will provide for you."
"I will provide for you" is וְכִלְכַּלְתִּי (*vechilkalti*) in the original, and it means literally "I will hold the whole of you up."
And then verse 12 has a sentence that is hard to read unmoved: "Behold, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth that speaks to you."
"My mouth" is פִי הַמְדַבֵּר (*pi hamdaber*) in the original — "it is my own mouth that is speaking."
What that sentence means is this: he is speaking Hebrew. In chapter 42 he used an interpreter. Now he does not.
A mother tongue he has not spoken in twenty-two years — and this is the day he uses it to talk to his brothers.
"He fell on his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him." (Genesis 45:14–15)

"Fell on … his neck" is וַיִּפֹּל עַל־צַוְּארֵי (*vayipol al-tzavrei*) in the original — and when Esau came running in chapter 33 and threw his arms around Jacob's neck, the text used exactly the same words.
Two generations of this family are reconciled by the very same gesture.
And the most important part is that last line: "After that his brothers talked with him."
In verse 3 they "couldn't answer him." By verse 15 they are finally speaking.

Brothers and sisters, the mark that a relationship has been restored is that the person starts talking to you again. Not one apology. Not one bout of tears. It is that from that day on, the two of you can talk properly again.
Then Joseph sends them home. He gives them clothing, he gives them wagons, he gives them provisions. And the last word of instruction he gives them is this:
"See that you don't quarrel on the way." (Genesis 45:24)

What a practical sentence that is. The road home takes several days, and somewhere along it they are certain to start doing the arithmetic: whose idea was it in the first place? Who laid hands on him first? Who was it that went and took that coat?
He says: don't. If people who have been forgiven turn round and start settling accounts with one another, that forgiveness has been wasted.

It is the same in the church. After God's forgiveness has come to a team, the easiest thing in the world is for the team to start apportioning blame inside itself. Joseph says: don't quarrel on the way.
How much weight does that word "a remnant" carry?

In the original it means what is left over, the ones who survive. This is the first seed of the Old Testament's whole theology of the remnant — Isaiah later, and Jeremiah, and Paul, all use this word for the small group God keeps for himself in the worst of years. So what God saves here is not only one man; it is a family. And not only a family; it is the Saviour who would one day come out of that family. That is a great comfort to anyone serving today in a small church or a small group: God's work usually does not run on numbers, it runs on the few he keeps. If it feels to you as though there are only a handful of you left, that may well be the most ordinary picture in the whole Bible.
They come back to Canaan and tell their father, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt."
"His heart fainted, for he didn't believe them." (Genesis 45:26)
"His heart fainted" is, in the original, literally "his heart went numb" — his heart stopped.
Twenty-two years. He has already wept for that son, already held the mourning, already said, "For I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." His heart scarred over on that matter long ago.
It is very hard to make a man who has grieved for twenty-two years believe a piece of good news. A human heart gets wrapped up and guarded by its own sorrow, and then even good news is kept outside.
"They told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them. When he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob, their father, revived." (Genesis 45:27)

"Revived" is וַתְּחִי (*vatechi*) in the original — literally, "it came alive again." That word "live" has been sounding all the way through this chapter, and at the end it comes to rest on the old father.
And what brought him back to life? Words, plus wagons. What he heard, plus what he saw.

Brothers and sisters, this is very often how God deals with us too. He gives us his word, and he also gives us evidence we can see. He sends people to come and fetch us; he does not simply tell us to make our own way over.
And then Jacob says the last sentence of the chapter:
"It is enough. Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die." (Genesis 45:28)
Notice what the text calls him. Verse 27 says "Jacob, their father." Verse 28 says, "Israel said."
In the very moment an old man hears the good news, the text hands him back the name God gave him.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This is the chapter of Genesis most easily misused, and there are several places you must be able to recognise.

The first distortion is taking "God meant it for good" and using it to comfort someone who is still inside the suffering. Joseph said that himself, twenty-two years afterwards; nobody said it on his behalf. Spoken too early, it is cruelty to a person in pain. The test is this: when the one who is hurting has heard you, does he feel accompanied, or does he feel dismissed?

The second distortion is preaching God's sovereignty in a way that makes human evil stop counting as evil. In verse 4 he says outright, "whom you sold into Egypt"; in chapter 50 he says, "you meant evil against me." Both sentences must be present together. The test is very simple: when the congregation has heard you, is sin still sin?

The third distortion is preaching forgiveness as though everything must be restored to what it was, immediately. Joseph watched them for two whole chapters and made sure they had changed before he made himself known. Preach instant reconciliation and you will push victims who are still in danger back into it. Forgiveness can be a decision one person makes alone; reconciliation takes two.

The fourth distortion is skipping over "See that you don't quarrel on the way." If people who have been forgiven turn round and start settling accounts with one another, that forgiveness has been wasted. It is a very practical warning. Do not skip it.

The fifth distortion is preaching "cause everyone to go out from me" as if it meant that family shame must never be aired in public. What Joseph protected was his brothers' dignity, not their sin; to their faces he set the facts out with complete clarity. The difference between covering sin and protecting dignity is this: has the truth been said out loud? Protecting dignity says it — it simply refuses to humiliate a person in front of a crowd.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: we are very good at not tearing the surface of a relationship, and we are just as good at talking behind people's backs. On the surface everything is pleasant and courteous; we turn around and say to somebody else, "Do you know what he did back then?" Brothers and sisters, Joseph did precisely the opposite: to their faces he said it plainly, and behind everybody's back he protected their dignity. This week I am asking you to run one check. That matter — when was the last time you told somebody about it? If you are still passing on the story of another person's humiliation, that forgiveness is not finished. This week, do not bring that old matter up in any setting at all.

The second question: in our families there is very often a heart that has gone cold. It may be an elder who shut his heart over something that happened years ago; it may be ourselves, hurt once and now not daring to believe even good news. How did Jacob's heart come alive again? Words, plus wagons — somebody kept on talking, and somebody drove the wagons up to the door. Brothers and sisters, if there is a heart like that in your family, do not rush it, and do not scold it with "why are you so faithless?" What you have to do is keep speaking, and drive the wagons over. Some hearts only come alive once they have seen.
7. Living 321 Out — Letting Him Decide How I Read My Own Past
Brothers and sisters, let us carry this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. When Joseph said, "Come near to me, please," it was the wronged party who moved first. And the risen Lord, standing in front of disciples who had run away and denied him, said, "Peace be to you." And on the shore he said, "Come and eat breakfast!" My role model is this: he walks over first, and then he asks me to come near.

The Bible is my standard. The standard is not "there is no hatred in my heart, so that will do." The standard is: "be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you." Feeling says that cutting the person off is enough; the standard says forgiveness is putting the person back into the relationship.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to make yourself known and when to go on waiting — that is a question of guidance. Joseph waited two chapters. Too early, and the other side is not ready; too late, and the door has closed. To rely on our intellect and lean on ourselves ends in worry; to rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit ends in gladness.

Let Jesus be King. "It wasn't you who sent me here, but God." Letting Jesus be King means letting him decide how I read my own past. One and the same stretch of life: I can read it as "I was destroyed", or I can read it as "God sent me before you." Whoever holds the right to interpret your life is your king.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. He says, "God has made me lord of all Egypt." He does not say, "I climbed up here by myself." A man who has handed God the right to interpret his past will hand God the credit for his present as a matter of course.

Establish God's system. "God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance." What God saves is not only one man; it is a whole family. To establish God's system is to keep many people alive — and that stretch of suffering you went through may well have been so that many people can live later on.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "I Am Joseph"
We are standing in that room with four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "I can forgive him, but first he has to understand how badly he was in the wrong." Joseph held every card. He could have nailed them up in public. Instead he sent the outsiders away. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights; it insists that the other man kneel first. Humility is returning to our originally intended position as a human being and saying, "Come near to me, please."

The fearful heart says, "If I forgive him, will he simply do it again?" That is an entirely legitimate concern. So pay attention to Joseph's order: he watched them for two chapters, saw that they had genuinely changed, and only then made himself known. Forgiveness is not the same as dropping your guard. Forgiveness is that I let go inside; the boundary can still stand.

The ashamed heart says, "Now that he knows the truth, I cannot face him." That was them too — they were too terrified to speak. And what Joseph said was, "Don't be grieved, nor angry with yourselves." Brothers and sisters, to go on condemning yourself after you have been forgiven is to disbelieve the forgiveness. God has forgiven; you are to follow him and let it go.

The wounded heart says, "Twenty-two years — who is going to pay me back?" Joseph never received compensation. What he received was a father still alive, a company of brothers who had turned round, and an account of his own life that he could finally say out loud. There are debts that cannot be settled on this earth. But there is One who will settle them, and he settles them more justly than we would.
Four kinds of heart, and one sentence: "I am Joseph." And in the Gospels there is another who stood in front of his disciples and said: look at my hands and my feet — it is I myself.
"Don't be grieved, nor angry with yourselves" — who is that said to?

It is said to the offenders. The root behind "grieved" is the very word for the "pain" laid on Adam and Eve under the curse in chapter 3; and "angry with yourselves" is literally "let it not burn in your eyes," that is, do not be furious with yourselves. There are people who, once they have been forgiven, find that the hardest person to let off is themselves — and Joseph thought even of that for them. That is very useful in pastoral work. Someone who has genuinely confessed will often fall next into a long season of punishing himself, and that does not make anybody holier; it only paralyses him. So the announcement of forgiveness has to be made in full: not only has your sin been forgiven, you may also stop punishing yourself.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do
First, before God. That speech you have been rehearsing inside for years — the "one day I am going to say this to his face" speech — hand it over to God, and stop rehearsing it.
Second, with yourself. Check whether you are still passing on somebody's humiliation. If you are, own it before God, and then stop.
Third, towards people. For someone who once hurt you, do one thing that protects his dignity. It might be saying a fair word for him in front of others; it might be never raising that matter again.
Fourth, in your daily living. This week, do not bring that old matter up in any setting. Not once.
Fifth, for your mission. Go to somebody whose heart has gone cold and tell him one piece of real good news. And do not only say it — if you can, drive the wagon up to his door.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who was sold by his own brothers, and twenty-two years later he was the ruler of that country. Second: when they were standing in front of him, he sent every outsider out of the room, and then he said, "Come near to me, please." Third: I have never forgotten it — real forgiveness protects the other person's dignity.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer delete that person from my heart; forgiveness is putting him back into the relationship.
I declare that that matter is no longer material for my conversation; I will protect the other person's dignity.
I declare that I hand the right to interpret my past over to God; it wasn't them, but God.
I declare that I will not quarrel on the way; people who have been forgiven do not settle accounts with one another.
If I am going to make that long-postponed telephone call this week, how do I begin?

Follow the order of this chapter. First, clear the room: not while other people are around, not in a group chat — one to one. Second, let your first sentence be about the relationship, not about the case — "I've been missing you", or "there's something I've wanted to say to you for a long time." Third, state the facts plainly, but only your own part of them; do not pass sentence on the other person. Fourth, say something that is an invitation, like that line "Come near to me, please" — "could we see each other again?" And last, accept that he may not be ready. What you can decide is to open the door. You cannot decide when he walks through it.

The door is shut, and the outsiders have all gone out. A man who holds the power of life and death over a whole country weeps aloud in his own house, and then speaks two words in his own tongue: I am Joseph.
And the next thing he asks is: does my father still live?

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. Because we too have once stood in front of someone like that — someone holding all the evidence, all the authority and every good reason; and he cleared the room, and said, "Come near to me, please," and then said: I am not here to condemn you, I am here to bring you home to the Father. He did not collect on that debt, because he had already settled it at the cross.

May God bless every one of us to become people willing to protect another's dignity; may the places in us that have gone cold come alive again; and may we be able to say, all our lives long, about our own past: it wasn't them, but God. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ The first mark of forgiveness is that it protects the other person's dignity. Run the check with your mouth: are you still telling other people what he did?
2. ★★ Deleting a person from your heart is severance, not forgiveness. Which relationship of yours does that distinction touch?
3. ★ Human evil is real evil, and God's sovereignty is still greater. Why must those two sentences be said together?
4. ★★ "Don't be grieved, nor angry with yourselves" is said to the offenders. Why do forgiven people go on punishing themselves?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentences for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (he is the one who ought to come to me), fearful (I am afraid it will only be more awkward once I speak), ashamed (I am the one who did wrong), wounded (I waited twenty years and never got an apology). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Come near to me, please." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there someone you have already deleted from your heart but have not forgiven? What is it you are guarding against?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The call I have never made is to …"
9. ★★ This week, will you make that call or send that message? Say out loud the first sentence you will use.

Leader's reminder: never use "God meant it for good" to hurry anybody into forgiving — that sentence can only come out of the mouth of the person it happened to. If someone is not yet ready, affirm his honesty, and stay with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there something you are still using as material for conversation? How will you stop it this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your service, whose embarrassment do you most often open with?
12. ★★★ The practice of invitation: this week, swap one command for an invitation (for example, change "you ought to come" into "I would like you to come"). Say who you will say it to.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him about the call you mean to make, and ask him at the end of the term whether you made it. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who was sold into slavery by his own brothers, and twenty-two years later he was the ruler of the country, with those brothers standing in his power. Second: he sent every one of his officials out of the room, shut the door and wept aloud, and the first words he said were, "I am Joseph. Does my father still live?" Third: so what I learned is that the first step of forgiveness is refusing to let that matter go on being other people's talk. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the person you have deleted but not forgiven, and the first sentence you will say this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep us from making other people's wounds into conversation, and to give us the gentleness to say, "Come near to me, please."
